utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, you are to commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness E.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Dusan Vucicevic. I'm an attorney from Chicago, and I represent Dragan Kolundzija in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Our headsets don't appear to be working and although I can hear Mr. Vucicevic, I don't anticipate I will be able to hear the witness' answer. Nothing is working on our control panel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us have that matter checked. Is it working now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This panel still doesn't, but I have an alternate one that will work. The usher has solved our problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm just going to say that the panel still doesn't work but the usher has fixed our problem. We have an alternate source of input, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness E, you testified yesterday that you were arrested by soldiers and also after some detour, you were taken to Keraterm where you noticed the soldiers who have checked you out, frisked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers, the guards, those who were with us who escorted the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You also testified when you came to the Keraterm, you did not know anybody who was there. Were those men who were there soldiers, but not the guards that came a few days later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not notice -- you didn't see Kole there when you came. So you saw Kole a few days later. If you could approximately say how many days later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to ask you just quickly a few questions that you have testified about yesterday, and to amplify them some. You said that you never saw any beatings, torture, killings, or any mistreatment of prisoners on Kole's shift; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, on Kole's shift there was several things that were done throughout which made your stay there somewhat easier; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You testified about your brother and you using the phone, but somehow the transcript showed that it was only you and your brother that used the phone. You meant the other people used the phone also.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: On how many occasions have you used the phone on Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once or maybe twice, twice, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And if you -- if we take as a reference point, the beating that you suffered by Crni on his shift, was the first time that you used the phone before you were beaten up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I'm not sure. I don't know exactly. No, I did not use the telephone after I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether your brother had used the phone to inform your family that you are doing well, whatever it means under the circumstances of your confinement, but that you are still alive after the shooting on Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me move to food and water supplies. Are you aware that Kole took several prisoners on many occasions to the water well in the neighbourhood to fetch some cold, clean water for drinking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about it, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Kole took a few inmates home to change, to see their families and they brought them back home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If you know, who were those inmates? Would you please state their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names. I just know them very superficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It was very unusual and nobody has ever expected that something like that could happen in Keraterm; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You remember that Kole had given food which was delivered to the guards but that was not consumed by the guards, that he had given to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please describe where was the food, that food for the guards, delivered? Where was it taken, and how were the prisoners selected who were -- who were fed with that additional food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how they were getting their food. I really couldn't remember that. But he would give the food and then tell those young lads and said, "Give it to those young lads." You know, there were some young lads, 14, 15 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Your recollection on that point is just enlightening the court and all of us, but another point, if you could remember, was he, Kole, selecting those men or he had allowed the inmates to select them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you saw Zigic came once or so on Kole's shift but he didn't beat anybody at that time, didn't abuse anybody at all; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember all of that now because it was a long time ago, and one simply forgets things after all that time. Maybe he did come. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was indeed a long time ago, and I appreciate your answer. You said that -- when you testified on direct, and that was yesterday, in the transcript that is page 59, line 4, you said that you saw Kole on the night, on 24th of July, when he took over the shift; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which date it was. I'm not sure about the date because we did not know the dates. I only know that Kole once took over the shift and locked the dormitories around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So when you saw Kole that night, where was he standing when you saw him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the door. He locked the door, he left, and then we couldn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So that -- isn't it true that that evening, and that afternoon, the door of your room was open?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: At night? You mean at night?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: No, what I --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 10.00 the door was always locked. Commanders locked the door to avoid then something happening or prevent somebody coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. My question then just logically follows. If that was locked at 10.00, it was open prior to that and it was open throughout the early evening and throughout the day; that's true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And in your statement that you have given to the Office of the Prosecutor dated August 15, 2000, which you have read -- strike it -- which was read to you in Bosnian, and it was true, which you had signed, and I'm going to read it to you in Bosnian because I have a Bosnian version here. You said: [Interpretation] "I did not see before the massacre of people in Room 3 any -- I did not see any preparations before the massacre of people in Room 3." [In English] You said that in -- on August 15, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose I did, if it says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Since that was just an ordinary day, on that day, you went out to drink water, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, prior to the incident in Room 3, the shooting at Room 3, since that was an ordinary day, you went out to drink some water throughout that day, any time from early in the morning until the time that the doors were locked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say, really, because I just don't know exactly. I don't remember. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And on that day, being that it was an ordinary day, you went out to have the meal, that one meal that was delivered to you once a day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And that meal was just delivered as on any other day, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that it was every day because at times there was no electricity, so sometimes it was delayed, but it was usually around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So do you remember whether there was any electricity in Keraterm compound on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember -- no, no, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And the only way that you could know whether there was electricity or not, it was according to the water that was pumped out of the hydrants; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. I do not know how they pumped the water or where they did it from. At times the hydrant would drip without electricity of anything. But more or less, yes, at that time when there was electricity, there was water too usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So Witness E, I'm just trying to kind of, you know, put some landmarks here for Court to, you know, understand what was happening there. And if there was anything else that -- throughout daytime, any other indicators throughout the daytime that could tell you whether there was electricity, please help us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think that there was electricity then because we had electricity very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So do you remember then whether you received water on that day by means of water tank, tanker truck, that was delivering that water very frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the tanker from the public utilities company 4th of July, and at times it would come from the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So in order to know there were no water -- there was no water on that day, and to have received the food, you had to go out of the room on that day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't understand. Could you please reword it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You have already testified that you had taken some food on that day that, you know, that there was no electricity on that day because there was no water there. So in order to have seen all of this, you had to come out and walk in front of Room 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see, when you went out, any prisoners being beaten in front of -- on the grass in front of the Rooms 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Any time throughout that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't remember that. I don't think so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So that's why you said it was just one of those ordinary days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what an ordinary day is to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You also testified that after the door was locked, you fell asleep; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether the voice is cutting here but my microphone is coming -- not microphone, but earphones are coming on and off. It might be a lose contact. If everything is okay, I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the registrar aware of a problem, a technical problem? No, we are not aware of any problems. I think you should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And you felt so secure that you could go to sleep on that evening. Kole's shift was on. There was nothing to worry. As usual, you could go to sleep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was there, we could have some rest and get some sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you try to remember what exactly woke you up and at what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm able to fix the time, but I think it must have been after midnight, but was it 1.00 or 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning, I couldn't say. We were woken up by a song from dormitory 3, and they were singing, "Who is saying? Who is lying? Serbia is small." That is what we heard, and that is what woke us up, because they were singing loudly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And there was a -- also a rancor or a quarrel and a fight among the men in Room 3 because that was a really thin wall between those two rooms? You could hear it, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what went on there, be they have a fight or what. I couldn't -- you can hear some things. You can hear people talking at the top of their voices or yelling. But why they were doing that, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: While they were yelling, could you hear, "We want to break out, we don't have air"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you indicated -- that you have given in 1995, you indicated that you were beaten up 42 days after your confinement in Keraterm. How did you -- this is not -- nothing to trick you, just to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 inform us all. How did you ascertain that number, 42? You must have been counting the dates, marking them somehow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we all counted days as of our arrival in the camp. That was the only thing. Otherwise, there was no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you are certain that Crni was still a shift commander at that time? You testified so, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You have testified already that Crni, the shift commander who called you out of the room and then who was present while you were beaten, that he was indeed a shift commander on that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was he who -- no, believe me, I really don't know whether he was the true shift commander. It was from what I saw, how he behaved, and what he did that I perceived him as such, but he was the one who took me away, and he beat me, he, Keli, and that pilot whom I know. That is, I only know that he was called a pilot. And the remaining three that were there, I did not know them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when you were cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic, you said that at the beginning there were two shifts and commander of one shift was Crni. So do you change your mind from yesterday to today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It is in the transcript. You, in your -- in your statement that you've given to the OTP on August 15, 2000, you have testified that you had had conversation with Kole after the shooting on Room 3. How many days after; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Where did it take place, on what location in camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhere in front of the dormitories, between the third and the fourth dormitory. We sat on the curb next to the asphalt path.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And it wasn't only you and Kole sitting, but there were other men sitting there around Kole? That was the first time when Kole came back; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether there was anybody else there. I know I talked with him, and I asked him for cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So doesn't that indicate that Kole is very good friend of yours when, after such a terrible occurrence, that you and him would sit alone to have a chat about it? Or perhaps there were the other people who knew him so well and they were around, but you perhaps don't remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a closed session, please -- private session for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You sat on the grass in front of Room 3, and this is how you stated that it is happened when Kole told you this. "I don't know what happened, but had I been there, it would not have happened."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Objection in the translation. Not"there", here. I'll read it again. [Interpretation] "I don't know what happened, but had I been here, it would not have happened."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Had I been here, it would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... that's what you just heard, because if you heard anything else, you would have testified about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: There is no answer on the transcript, Your Honour, that's why I am pausing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness E, what is the answer to the question? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness answered "Yes, absolutely," but somehow it didn't get on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said, Witness E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether it was true that this was the only thing he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, "Absolutely."

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness E. So since Kole was sitting on the place where the shooting -- where the shooting took place from or close thereabouts, he might have referred, if he was there, right on that spot where you were. He didn't say, "If I was in town," or, "If I was in camp." He just said, "If I was here." So that could have meant that one and you didn't inquire about anything else; is that correct? A possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That, again, is for argument, not for speculation by the witness. All the witness can testify to is to what he heard said. He shouldn't be asked to speculate about what was going on in Kole's mind at the time. That's for argument by counsel, in our respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond to this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I think there was only one word here that has to be explained, and that one word was -- it's a general word, and I'm asking the witness to explain how he understood it, and what that word could have meant at that time. That's all what I'm asking. I'm not suggesting. I'm not testifying. I'm not putting any words in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, you may ask the witness what he, the witness, understood it to mean, not what he understood Kole to mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- by the statement. Let's try to move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is going to be my last question. I just have another cite here so that the witness is going to be in a better position to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness E, you have testified yesterday, and you have precisely used these words, [Interpretation] "Kole told me had I been here, nothing would have happened." [In English] But in your statement of August, you said something different, something similar. Not exactly the same words, different words. You said -- and I'm citing in Bosnian: [Interpretation] "I don't know what happened, but had I been here, it would not have happened." [In English] So you did not repeat word to word what Kole said. That was your general recollection for what he said; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me it all -- it is all the same, the way I see it. "Had I not been here," or "if I were here," or the third one, I don't know. It's all more or less the same. It depends on how people express themselves, but grammatically speaking, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And after he said this to you, you didn't ask him one single question, what did he mean by this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall now, but this was a long time ago, 1992, nine years ago, almost nine years ago. We can say it's nearly nine years. I cannot recall every word I exchanged with him, how long I spoke. I remember that I asked him for cigarette and I remember that we talked about this, what these words reflect. If I remembered anything more, I would have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something else. You were testifying yesterday that various people, a lot of people, maybe six, seven, were tortured and killed in Keraterm. Isn't it true that none of these people were killed on Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the massacre which took place, I am unaware of anybody being touched or beaten. I don't know. I cannot guarantee about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You also testified that the people that were selected as the punishment group, they were deemed to be extremists; isn't that true? These are all the things that you said now, because, you know, we can go quickly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people -- you asking about the people who were called extremists?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called them extremists. I don't know who it was who named them extremists, but in reality, they called them people for special treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Those are all the things that you testified yesterday, and I don't have any dispute with them. I'm just asking you to affirm that Serb authorities at that time called extremists those ones that took arms to fight them actually in attack on Prijedor or liberation of Prijedor. It all depends which side we are on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: They considered all people who were in the SDA extremists. Those who were not with the SDS, to them they were all extremists, some to a lesser, some to a greater degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But those ones that had arms or that were caught with arms right after attack on Prijedor, they were certainly considered extremists, so we can let those ones, just regular members of SDA, aside from the time being. Those ones that had arms in their hands were considered extremists, that's for sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who had weapons, nor whom they considered to have had weapons or to have been extremists. There were a lot of hunters in our midst. They had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I was not about ever to ask you that question because you were -- never testified or said that you were involved yourself in looking who had weapons, so we will not go there, Mr. Witness E. Could I have -- I have an exhibit, please. Mr. Witness E, I would like you to look at this document, to read these names, and to tell me, do you know whether any of these people are well and living today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the first -- top two, that they are alive. I don't know about the rest. Bakir Hrncic, who left with me in Travnik, and Malik Hrncic, whom I found in Travnik when I crossed Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just follow this up. Has any of these men spent time in Keraterm that you know of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Edin Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And is he alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but he was a fireman.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The one that was arrested with you that had the cakija in his pocket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. As long as we are at that term, I think you ought to explain to the court what cakija really means, because it was talked about that yesterday and that is a pocket knife typical for Bosnia; isn't that correct? But pocket knife, this is about ten centimetres long, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: About this, there was some that are smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Usually -- and usually does have a blade which is just that long too, just as the handle is on one side and the blade forward. And the blade is about one and a half to two centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a folding knife, I think you might call it, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It's a folding knife, but I haven't seen it any place in the west, and it's kind of typical. Because what I am going to ask him now you will see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Because this is a knife which is sometimes used to slaughter a pig or slaughter a lamb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to these names. If -- could you read, there is handwriting on the B/C/S and it reads, "The group which participated in the attack against Prijedor on May 30th, 1992." So if there is a name or two here that I know of, and that the Prosecutor knows of that survived, perhaps there are some other ones that survived also; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excuse me, what kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to mention any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I just don't understand the relevance of that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 question to this witness. If my friend, again, wants to make this as an argument, I just don't know how this witness can be of assistance to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this question of survivors?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Because if the man who has survived has been caught with a weapon in his hands and he has survived, then perhaps he might revise his statement what extremists are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll allow it. Proceed quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If a man who is on this list has been caught with a weapon in his hands and he had survived, perhaps your view of what extremists are or your view of what Serbs considered extremists should be somewhat narrower, shouldn't be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say something if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we have to finish this. Because you only know one man here, and I'm saying if that man had some arms and survived, then your -- what you said before what Serbs considered extremist should be modified, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer that question, Witness E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Tepic, he didn't have any weapons and there are other Tepics and the father's name is different. So I cannot even say who this one is. I know that the name is familiar. I did not say that I knew the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have explored this point sufficiently. Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that Car was one of those killed early on. Did you know him before the war or knew him by sight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him. I don't know what his profession was. We knew each other superficially in the cafes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... once and a while in a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: With him, his brother, his sister. Occasionally I also met his father. We called them all Car. That was a nickname for all of them except for his sister whose name I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... reasonably to say that you knew him well because you knew the whole family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know all of them, but I knew part of the family. One of the brothers worked as a waiter in the bar called Jedinica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: His name was Jusufovic Sead, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact full name, but I only know that his nickname was Car.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But you couldn't -- you were not drinking with him regularly. You were drinking with him on and off. You would see him, but then he wouldn't be there, but you would see him, but he wouldn't be there. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And that is the reason because he has been constantly in trouble with the law in the years prior to the war, wasn't it? He's been in court in and out for ten years.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that he had -- was in trouble with the law was no reason for anyone to kill him. There is law to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I certainly agree with you. I mean I couldn't agree with you any more. But I'm just asking whether he had this reputation of being a criminal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what criminal may mean for someone. I don't know his dealings with the police, with the judiciary. That, I don't know. We only knew each other superficially. I knew his father who was also Car. He had a leg missing. And all the male members of that family we called Car.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I have something that might help refresh his recollection. That is a rap sheet from the Prijedor police station indicating about all the convictions that that man has had, if he can read it and refresh his recollection. If it refreshes his recollection that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With respect, if I understand the witness' evidence, he says he knew nothing of it. To show him a document now in the hopes it may refresh recollection, there has to be recollection to be refreshed. And from what I understand the witness to say, he knows nothing about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, you can produce that through another witness. The witness has said that he has no recollection. So produce that document through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really appreciate your ruling and I will certainly do that. However, I am a little perturbed that when we are -- when my learned friend is making these statements, that is not being referred to the transcript and to the line. Because if I am going to my recollection when I agreed absolutely with the witness, the witness said, "So what if he was a criminal, what has it to do with him being killed," and I agree with him. That is horrendous. It shouldn't have happened. But, you know, if we are going to have this colloquy with witness being present, then it becomes, you know, -- it's not a side bar but I do thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vucicevic, the document that you showed the witness, what do you intend to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I would respectfully ask you to admit it as Kolundzija Defence Exhibit number 1 because that was a document that was already pre-admitted by -- a document that was produced by the Prosecutor and I would just like it to be admitted into trial evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No objection whatsoever. As a matter of fact, I think that document may already be part of the binder that has, as I understand it, already been admitted in evidence by some other number as part of the Prosecution's case. But I have no objection to it going in or being referred to by a Defence exhibit number should that be the court's wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it as Defence Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D1/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness E, that concludes your testimony. You are released.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Before we call the next witness, Your Honour, there is an issue I would like to raise, if I may, before we call the next witness. Do you want me to wait until the witness leaves the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will just wait until he leaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected earlier to ask the court's permission for one of our investigating officers, who is on our witness list, to be permitted to either watch the proceedings by some means? As I understand it, there is a practice that has developed at this Tribunal that in the event there are potential witnesses on the list who happen to be investigators, that we should be seeking the court's permission to allow them to either from time to time view the proceedings, or to watch it by closed circuit transmission on the television broadcast. I might say that this witness is on our witness list, near the very end of the list, for the sole purpose of assisting the court with respect to the exhumation areas, some of the reports that are being put in, and this investigator, of course, is important to us, to be of assistance to us throughout the course of the trial. It's my understanding that other courts have granted such permission, and I have simply forgotten up until now to make an application for the court's consent. I don't know whether my friends take objection to this matter but that is my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are there some rules on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My understanding is there is not a rule per se, but it is certainly within our policy that we are to ask the court's permission. I suppose there is technically an issue as to a matter of weight to be placed on that witness' evidence. My understanding is there is a rule that just because a witness may have heard evidence or have been present in the courtroom does not preclude him from being able to give evidence, but it's always a matter of weight. This is something that's quite different. He will be dealing with the issue of exhumation reports and perhaps being asked some questions. He may not be called but he is on our witness list [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, before you begin, let me deal with this. As far as the rules are concerned, I think they are silent, but you can tell me if I'm wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I believe that to be the case. I'm aware of the practice that has developed in some cases. I'm not sure that all cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was going to say certainly in cases which I've been in we have allowed the investigator into court in these circumstances. Thinking aloud about it, the objection can only be if it might affect his evidence, and if it's on a limited area, I don't know what that objection can be, if it's really --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I offer another problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Which is if that investigator is going to be engaged in the proofing of future witnesses, or is going to be briefing other investigators on the proofing of witnesses, that would be undesirable. It's got to be somebody who is independent of that process, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I could add one other thought. It may be that, in due course, the Defence will want their investigator in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is of course that. We have much more limited resources than the Office of the Prosecutor and are only allowed to have one investigator, so that the objection that I've raised is a problem for us. I hope I'm speaking, as it were, more as amicus curiae than making a specific objection. I'm just concerned that an investigator can be sitting there watching how the Defence is trying to develop its case and in some ways influencing witnesses. That's something we ought to try and avoid. It's a danger. It's not a specific allegation, I hasten to add, but it can be done unconsciously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any other counsel wish to speak on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not wish to waste your time but I fully endorse Mr. Greaves's objection. I think equality of arms might be brought into question if Prosecution's investigator were allowed to be present whereas we are not. Rather we simply cannot for various reasons to bring in an investigator, even tender documents through him, let alone something more, let alone have him admitted to the courtroom or admitted to the proceedings or to respond, to use on the ground what he heard in the courtroom, to be present in the courtroom. So I'm afraid that Prosecution's investigator would seriously bring into question the equality of arms, which is always at peril.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I wasn't suggesting that the Prosecution would be allowed to have their investigator into court but you would not. What I was suggesting was that, in due course, you may want to have your investigator into court, in which case, of course, we would be no doubt minded to allow it if we had allowed the Prosecution investigator into court. The equality of arms would work in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would be the happiest if we could have our investigator present from the very beginning, equally as the investigator of the Prosecution, but the Registry does not allow that and explicitly forbids it. They do not allow us to have a legal adviser here or a legal assistant here, let alone an investigator. We accept with due respect what you are telling us and we accept that, but the Registry's practice is different. And as far as I know, it holds true of all the cases. No Defence team has had -- have had their investigators present in the courtroom or present at parts of the proceedings here. If I'm wrong, I stand to be corrected, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not my experience. I remember cases in which we have allowed the Defence investigator into court. But let's not argue about that. That's not the point at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I object on principle because in jurisdiction that I'm coming from, the very first motion at the beginning of the trial is motion to exclude witnesses. And if this man is -- or woman is going to be witnesses, then I would like them excluded. If they are going to testify about any particular matter, they have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... witnesses whom they are going to hear on their own because that's the witness they are going to produce anyway? So their presence in the courtroom is superfluous, you know. They want to waste their time, that's fine, but I think the principle is something that matters. There must be something else that he wants to find out. And that's what I'm wondering what it is. Coming about the equality of arms, with the highest regards for learned Judge May, we indeed, judge, don't have that equity of arms when it comes to the investigators. Might have been just an exceptional instance that it did happen, but it's impossible for us to have the investigation, the very nature of the organisation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, please slow down for the interpreter. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: They all sit here with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Switch on his microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And our investigators are in Bosnia and never come here, or very seldom, and, you know, it might have some theoretical implication but rather none practical. And equity of arms is a lot more practice than -- for us, theory is for the court and we appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, why do you need to have the investigator in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Not necessarily in court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I mean to hear the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, there are often situations where we are working on our closing brief that the officer may be of assistance to us. There are situations that need to be checked out. In other words, we don't have unlimited resources either. There are very few investigators, and those that have been assigned to us need to be available to us in order to assist us throughout the course of the trial. I might just say that when I made reference to my understanding of the Rule, I was referring -- I didn't have it out, but I've since looked, it was 90(D) that I had in mind when I made the application. And the witness would not be called as an expert so he would fall outside that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take time to consider this and give a ruling later. There is a matter I'd like to raise, it's the question of exhibits, and the requirement that exhibits be in both languages, both working languages, English and French. I want to remind both parties, although principally at this stage it might affect the Prosecution more directly than the Defence of this requirement, and it has to be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that the exhibits filed thus far are in English only and that there could be a considerable delay before we were able, physically, to have the interpreters who are busy, as I understand it. There are finite number of French interpreters, and they are backed up with doing judgements on other cases and other commitments. I realise that we are in trial and it is our obligation, but I'm just indicating to the Court that I see some practical difficulties as we speak in terms of getting those immediately to the Court. We'll have to make some extra special attempts to do that. Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have to work hard to meet this requirement because it is very important for the efficient functioning of the Court. Your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly will take this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is a witness for whom protective measures were granted on the 27th of December last year, they being a pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: We call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for the next witness will be Witness F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a look, please, at this piece of paper that you are about to be handed. On that piece of paper, do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you understand, Witness, that you, during these proceedings, are to be referred to as Witness F?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: That document is Exhibit 16.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, is it the case that you graduated from high school in 1984?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you completed a period of compulsory military service in an engineering unit in Karlovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: After your period of military service, were you unemployed for a couple of years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And in 1988, did you start to work as a taxi driver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to 1991. At that time did you own a cafe in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, live in the Puharska area in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: At the end of 1991, did you sell your cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Why did you sell your cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question. Well, the situation was such that one had to sell it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, the war was in the offing in that sense, and there was already war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Is it the case that there were elections held in Prijedor at the end of 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: At that time, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just an objection. I'm kind of here at loss. Witness is answering "Ja, Ja, Ja". That's not a word that's known in B/C/S, and translation is going "That's right. That's right." And that, as a matter of fact "J-a", it's a personal pronoun for the first indicating "I", like "I am in the courtroom." So I don't know what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for the elucidation. We rely on the interpreters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you interested in politics at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you, however, read newspapers and listen to the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Which radio did you listen to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Radio Prijedor, the local radio station. And naturally I watched television.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What newspaper or newspapers did you read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Kozarski Vijesnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you describe, briefly, the nature of that newspaper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was a local paper of the town that I lived in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: After the elections, did the population begin to gather on an ethnic or national basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can I take you now to the beginning of 1992. What was the situation insofar as politics and advertising politics on the -- through the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That -- I don't really know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did any of the political parties advertise their policies through either the radio, the newspaper, or the television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right, yes, they did mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just briefly, what were the political parties that existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: There were the SDA, SDS, and the HDZ in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Dealing firstly with the SDA, what type of a political party was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Most of these parties were ethnic parties. So the SDA was practically all Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what about the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That was the party of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Of the Croat one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And so far as advertising on the media is concerned, which party was it that used the media to advertise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: SDS by and large.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what kinds of things were being said by the SDS through the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, it was for the most part propaganda from the front lines in Croatia where the war was already on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what was the nature of that propaganda? What sorts of things were being said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, how shall I explain it now? Well, that one should go and wage war in Croatia, that the Croats, ustashas, would come and slaughter, something to that effect, that all the people had to be mobilised and go to fight in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move to another subject. Would it be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, yes, it would be. Witness F, we will now take a break and resume at 11.30. During the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, and that includes members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, with all due respect, because witness is feeling uncomfortable, if he may want to leave the jacket for the rest of the session or something, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That will be a matter for him to determine. Yes. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, can I take you now, please, to the 30th of April, 1992? Was that the day on which the Serbs took over the power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened in so far as the power of -- of Radio Prijedor and the newspaper were concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: After the takeover of power, they appointed their own people to all key positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In so far as the radio station that you listened to, that is Radio Prijedor, what happened in so far as that was concerned, after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was also -- it was also transferred to the Serb, I don't know how to put it, to the Serb authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what kinds of things were broadcast over the radio after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: From that day on, everything was only Serb propaganda. You could not hear anything else. Serbian songs, Serbian everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In so far as propaganda is concerned, was there any particular propaganda that was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. They were saying that everybody had to go to the war in Croatia, to defend Yugoslavia, in that sense that everybody had to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was the situation in so far as the newspaper that you read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The same. Everything was the same as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can I take you now to the period of late May or around the 23rd of May in particular? Did an incident take place in the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was the nature of that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Two Serb, I don't know what they were, policemen or civilians, were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was there anything announced on the radio concerning that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That the renegades at Hambarine had killed those two, I don't know what they were, policemen or civilians, but they were labelled as Muslim rebels.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was there any announcement over the radio in so far as weapons are concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. It was ordered that all the weapons that were there would be turned in and that some automatic rifles be returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, are you familiar with what is called a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I heard that such Crisis Staffs existed, but I did not know what their role was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say you heard that they existed, when did they come into existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, you mentioned earlier in your evidence that key positions were taken over by Serbs. Can you just please explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Before this takeover of power, there were the elections in which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 the SDA party won the majority. So from this party, these SDA people were appointed to the leading positions, and then after the takeover, the Serb or the SDA members got to these positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And when you refer to the leading positions or the key positions, what exactly, what precisely were those positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The president of the municipality, the police commander, the person the head of the health services, school services, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In relation to firstly the police commander, prior to the situation, the crisis, what was the ethnicity of the person who held that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What about after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was that the situation insofar as all of the positions that you've mentioned are concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, you, yourself, are a person of Muslim ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, after the takeover, you remained residing in the Puharska area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you watching what was going on in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What did you notice insofar as the population of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: What did I notice? The ethnic groups started separating out. The stratification started in town. The people with whom I socialised, I no longer socialised with, and other people did that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you notice Serbs dressed in uniforms in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise the nature of those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Those were military police, all kinds of uniforms. They were different.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What sorts of things did those persons do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: For the most part they walked around about town without doing anything, and most of them had come back from the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did they, on any occasions, attend the homes of persons who were of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Not with me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say not with you, did it occur with any other persons to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know what period you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, I'm referring to a period after the takeover and, in particular, after the incident in Hambarine, that is, late May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It depended on the part of town. This Keraterm camp was open and they started gathering there, the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And was that non-Serb population concentrated in a particular area of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. These areas were the outlying areas, the villages around town, and the town itself, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say they were gathering the non-Serb population, how were they doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I can say how they did it in my area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How did they do it in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Simply they -- armed soldiers entered the street and rounded up everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, were you yourself rounded up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you concerned, Witness F, that you would be rounded up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What did you do because of your concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: My Serb neighbour protected me and we hid at his place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: For how long did you hide at his place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: When it was over, we could go back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Are you able to put a date on when you say it was over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but it was over the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: At some stage, Witness F, were you in fact rounded up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you just describe to the court, please, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: An unknown person called me from the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks to report to the barracks for an information interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How did you receive that call? Was that on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I was simply -- they simply called me on the phone. I picked up the phone and I was told to report to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you in fact report to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was the name of that barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Zarko Zgonjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened after you reported to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I was met by a guard at the reception office and he told me to wait. Five or ten minutes later, a Golf vehicle came with a driver and an escort, and they drove me over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, where was that barracks in relation to the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Keraterm was on the Prijedor-Banja Luka road and the barracks was on the Prijedor-Bosanska Dubica road.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness F, is it the case that you have in fact drawn a sketch or a map indicating the position of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Not the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I show you, please, a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I have, Your Honours, copies of those -- of that map in both English and B/C/S. I apologise at this stage, Your Honours, I do not have a French translation of that document. It has been requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just before it's placed on the ELMO, Witness F, for how long did you remain at the army barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I did not enter the barracks at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened after you arrived at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I was met with a soldier -- by a soldier at the reception office, and five to ten minutes later, a driver and an escort arrived in a Golf vehicle, and then they took me to Keraterm. That is, to the military police building behind Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And, Witness F, in so far -- the map might be placed on the ELMO at this stage. Just look, please, Witness F, at the map. Is that a map that you in fact drew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: May we have the B/C/S version placed upon the ELMO? Do you see, Witness F, that upon that -- on that map, you've drawn a building or a square that has "VP1" written on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Is that the building to which you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: VP2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You see on that map, you've also drawn a building and you've marked it "VP2."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. That is where they brought me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What is VP1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: VP1 was the other military police facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did that facility afford a view of the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. From VP1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: From VP2 is it the situation that you couldn't see the camp because, in fact, VP2 was behind the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, but only from the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Only what from the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That was a building -- you could only see the back of the building. In other words, you were not able to see the inmates in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Are you saying, Witness F, that from the building you've marked VP2, that is the military building that you were taken, you could see the back of the Keraterm camp but not in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The two soldiers who had brought me, took me to their interrogator, to their commander whose name was Dragan Radetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Dragan Radetic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly, there is a question mark after VP1 and a slash, and also VP2 and a slash in the English version. Is there any significance to that question mark?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are translator's notes. I do intend to clarify with the witness at a later stage some of the markings on the document that appear to have been difficult to read to the translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know that person Radetic prior to arriving at the police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In what circumstances and how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Dragan Radetic was a lawyer in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What did Dragan Radetic do at that time, that is, when you arrived at the police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He was in that room in his office there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you go into the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. Those two soldiers brought me over to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what happened after you were taken over to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Nothing. He ordered me to sit down, and then he asked me where I was, what I did, where my car was, what party I had financed. Questions in that vein.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you answer his questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I had to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Why, Witness F, do you say you had to answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Because the guards were out there and he had all the power.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Insofar as your -- the questions you were asked about your car, can you expand, please, on that? What were you asked and what did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He asked me where my car was. I said that it was at home. And he said that this car would be taken away for the needs of the Serb military, that I had to turn it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you have your car keys with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you do something with your car keys at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I turned them over to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He sent me with the escort of two soldiers to go home and show them where the car was. Then we went to get the car, and I was brought back to Radetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say, "We went to get the car," who took the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: We drove there. We drove in their military vehicle there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what happened to your car after you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: They simply took my car away.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You said you were then taken back to Radetic. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Then he said that there would be no problems whatsoever, but that I had to stay in Keraterm in any event for one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: For one day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you go to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He directed me there with the -- and he sent one guard with me to escort me to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Going back for a moment, Witness F, did you ever get your car back? Have you ever had your car returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How did you get to Keraterm, did you walk or were you transported in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: On foot. The distance is a few hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The guard brought me to the corner of what has been marked on the sketch as Room 1. And he ordered me to report to the guards on duty there who were lined up in front of Room 3 as marked on the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of those guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I recognised the majority of those guards because I knew them before the war. I knew them from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you name, please, the guards that you recognised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. Zoran Zigic; Dusan Knezevic, Duca; Zoran Vokic; Zeljko Timarac; and a number of others whose first and last names I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How did you know this person Timarac before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I knew him from the town because it is a small town and practically everybody knew one another, and he also played football in a club.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What about the person Zoran Vokic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I also knew him. Well, we were friends before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the person Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I knew him because we worked together for a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What did he do prior to the conflict? What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Before the -- before it broke out, he was a taxi driver, and for a while, he worked in Pula, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What about the person Dusan Knezevic? How did you know him prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, same thing. I knew him by sight from various coffee shops and other places. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you were taken to the outside of Room 1, did you notice anything going on at that time in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was it that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: In front of Zigic and those others, inmates were lined up, and they were beating them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What were they beating them with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Baseball bats, batons, rods, hands, feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Whereabouts on the bodies of the inmates were they being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: All over.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: At that time, did you have any contact, that is when you first arrived in the camp, with Zoran Zigic, and if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. The guard who brought me there ordered me to report to them. That is, to cross the concrete pista and report to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you in fact do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say "them," to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
