utterances.text: I did not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were interviewed by some military interrogators at the hospital as to who had beaten you in Keraterm. That was only on one occasion when they made a visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: They had plainly come as a result of a request to investigate the incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No. What request?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we'll move on. Did the military investigators, military police come on any other occasion whilst you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Not to my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why did you tell the Tribunal in your handwritten statement then, Witness F, this: "The military police from Banja Luka came to interrogate us every day." Why did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Perhaps I wrote it that way. I may have been thinking about daily interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suggest that what you have just told us about the military interrogators coming only once and what is written in your handwritten statement, those two things are completely different, Witness F, and I suggest to you that you are, at best, exaggerating greatly in your evidence and at worst, you are simply lying to us, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No. That is your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour would just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: After you were beaten by Zoran Zigic on the 5th of July, Witness F, it was the following day that a doctor came and examined you, decided you should go to hospital, and you went to hospital almost immediately; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How soon after being examined did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The examination took place two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Between you being beaten and your going to hospital, were any other prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And they were taken out and beaten but none of them died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you hear of any of them dying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: People were dying every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As a result of those beatings, Witness F, did you hear of anybody dying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Many died due to beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness F, I think the question is quite clear. You've told us that between your beating and your being taken to hospital, that prisoners were taken out and beaten. The question is clear. Did you hear of any of those dying as a result? Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, they died.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many prisoners were beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Many, about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why, then, did you in your handwritten statement tell the Tribunal this? This comes immediately after you've described your own beating. "About 30 prisoners were beaten that night and a couple of them died from beating and internal bleeding." And then you name two doctors and said that "they came in the morning and found that all the inmates had died a natural death. The guards threw them on the garbage dump." Why did you put that in your handwritten statement, Witness F?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I thought it would be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just turning for a moment again to the detail of your newspaper interview and your beating. You told, did you not, the newspaper that you were accused of cooperating with the leadership of the SDA? You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Do I remember what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you remember telling the journalist, the one who published or got -- wrote the article, that you had been accused of cooperating with the leadership of the SDA? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Printing their propaganda material? Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He added that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He added that. Transporting food for rebel Muslims, together with another man? Do you remember that, telling him that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I did -- what I said was that I had been accused of that whilst being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what it says. "I was also accused of shooting at Serbs with a sniper and financing the SDA party in Prijedor." Did you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you tell the journalist this? "That was my indictment and Serb justice was done accordingly. For 74 days I was in the hands of Chetnik beasts. Today I cannot believe that I used to live with those people, socialise with them, and even had friends amongst them. They are sick people. It is some kind of genetic disorder." Did you tell the journalist that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you use the phrase "Chetniks" to describe people who were on the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you -- do you recall telling the newspaper journalist about the death of Mr. Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I just mentioned it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you told him some of the details of what you'd seen and how you'd seen it, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, as individual details. To him what was important was only the names of those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Regardless of what he thought was important, let's look at what you told him, Witness F. Did you tell him how you'd seen an older man through a hole in your sleeping room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that man personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that you'd seen him through a hole in your sleeping room? Is that how you told the journalist what you'd seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't remember what I told him, but I did see him, through a hole or from the pista where we were, but I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What size was this hole through which you saw Mr. Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The door to the dormitory was the size of the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So you're not talking about a hole, small hole in the wall, you're talking about a door, are you? That's what you call a hole, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I never said a hole. Everybody knows what a hole is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention the death of Mr. Dizdarevic in your handwritten statement, Witness F?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not think it important.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You plainly thought it important enough to put into your interview and to mention it to the Office of the Prosecutor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I knew of other cases which seemed better for the Prosecution than that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were anxious to become a witness in this case, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. And I will continue to testify in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why were you so anxious, if I may ask, please, Witness F, to become a witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Because I went through a great deal and I want it to come out. I want justice to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we go into closed session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now about the village or small town of Hambarine, Witness F.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you hear of or know of an attack which took place on some Serbs at a checkpoint manned by Muslims in that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you hear how many Serbs were killed as a result of that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It was said that there were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you also hear that as a result of that, a demand was made by the Serb authorities for the surrender of the people who'd carried out the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right. They issued an ultimatum to turn over the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: To turn over the weapons and the people or just weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Weapons. They said to turn over the weapons and issue them with an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And was that ultimatum, as you understand it, and you have heard, the cause of the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That's right, yes, something like that. But I had nothing to do with this ultimatum because I lived in a completely different part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you did have anything to do with it, Witness F. Don't misunderstand me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: You asked me if I had something to do with the ultimatum. I think that was the question or the drift of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm not going to argue about that. Between the takeover and the date of your arrest, Witness F, some assistance was given to you by some people. They were of Serb ethnicity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: When they were rounding up people in my part of the town, yes, they helped me. They were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Turning now to the time of your arrival at Keraterm, initially it's right, isn't it, that Zoran Zigic prevented your -- stopped anybody from beating you at that point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Knezevic hit me straight away, and Zigic told me [as interpreted] not to touch me because I was his. Now, what he meant by this word "his" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You told us in evidence that you had seen other detainees being beaten upon their arrival at that point, and that that was done with the following implements, Witness F: Batons, baseball bats, rods, hands, and feet. Why did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor in the year 2000 that you could see how other guards beat prisoners with their batons in the vicinity? In other words, why have you now added all those other implements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Because I remembered that they were also used then. I stand by that, that they were also used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, may we go very briefly into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now about the water truck, please, Witness F, that was kept at Keraterm. It's right, isn't it, that there was a regular supply of water using that water truck; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. The water truck brought the water, but there were also hydrants in the compound from which water could also be used. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And so the detainees were able to use the water from the water trucks and had no restriction on use of the water hydrants; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, there were certain restrictions as far as hydrants were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as food was concerned, where was food prepared, Witness F?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The food was prepared outside the camp. It was brought there, and we heard -- we heard that it was prepared in the canteen of the Ljubija mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can go to ten past 4.00 with the cooperation of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hadn't been actually watching the time, and I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness F -- I'm sorry, just give me a moment please, Your Honour. No question of the kitchens at Keraterm being used. The food came from outside the camp prepared by others who were not at the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you explain then, please, why you said in your handwritten statement this: "We were fed once a day with a piece of bread and .2 of a litre of cabbage or bean soup. Sometimes the kitchens would not work because of power cuts so that we got our food once every day, every two days," implying, I suggest, that the food was being prepared on the premises. Why did you say that in your handwritten statement, Witness F?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Not the kitchen in the compound, a kitchen in the town. There was no kitchen in the compound. The town was without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like just now to return, please, if we may to the killing of the man called Dizdarevic. As far as you could tell, was that man killed off the premises of Keraterm, off the grounds of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I cannot be absolutely sure, but he was killed outside the Keraterm camp, next to the reception hut. Whether it was in front of the camp or inside, but it was right next to the reception hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So let's just be absolutely clear. You cannot say whether it was inside or outside the perimeter that that killing took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I did not see him being killed. I heard about it, and he -- but his sons said that he had been killed because he never came back and all trace of him is missing, and his sons were with me in the camp, and we all watched as he would ride on his bicycle past the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So you cannot say, either of your own observation or of your own knowledge, whether it was somebody on the camp staff who killed him or somebody who was not part of the camp staff, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Well, there were guards at the entrance into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Please answer the question, Witness K. You'll get away from here a lot quicker if you listen to the question and answer the question which you have been asked. I'll repeat it for you. You cannot say, can you, either from your own observation or from knowledge given to you, whether it was somebody on the camp staff or somebody who was not on the camp staff who carried out the killing. You simply cannot say, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I cannot, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The people who administered the beating to you were all people who came from outside the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who do you say of those was somebody who was inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Zoran Karlica or Goran Karlica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I turn now, please, to your interrogation and indeed interrogations in general? When you were interrogated in Keraterm, did you know the names of the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I knew names. I even knew some of those investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were they people who were part of a group who were designated as specialist interrogators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a specialist group of people who were civilian policemen who were designated as interrogators at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes. Above Room number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The people who interrogated you, did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What were the names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Bane Siljegovic, Branko Bucalo and others elude me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you please help Their Honours about this, Witness F? You've just told us that you knew the names of them. Why did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor in September 2000 this: "After ten days I was taken back to the Keraterm camp and interrogated. I did not know the names of those interrogators." Why did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor that, if you did, in fact, as you've now told us, know the names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I learned them later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Since September, 2000? You've learnt the names since September, 2000? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What did you mean by, "I learned them later on," then, Witness F?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: After that first interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, when you made your handwritten statement in January, 1998, you were able to tell the Tribunal this: "Apart from the guards at the camp, there was a special interrogation commission made up of civilian policemen. Their task was to gather data on all prisoners. They processed all the prisoners." And then you named four people. Now, help us again. Is it a case of you having forgotten in the meantime, when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, who had interviewed you, who had interrogated you, and you've now remembered again? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The problem is, Witness F, you can't get your story right two occasions running, can you, because you're not being very truthful with this Tribunal, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That is what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The guard who escorted people to the interrogations, did you know that person by name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was it obvious from what you could see of him that he was somebody who was from a separate unit from the personnel of the -- of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He wore the uniform of the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now briefly to the incident of the killings at Room 3, Witness F. Would you accept this, that prior to it happening, you heard Kolundzija, Kole, with soldiers who had come from outside the camp and he was arguing with them? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you heard specifically this, Kole saying, "I cannot let this happen."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: One could hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you overhear one of the soldiers from outside the camp saying that they would take full responsibility for what was about to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: One could hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you also hear during the shooting Kole, at some distance from you, telling them not to shoot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: On -- at number 1, "Don't shoot at number 1."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I now ask you, please, about the day after that incident? You claim that you were outside during the course of the day following. Apart from those you have already discussed, did you see somebody called Zivko Knezevic in the camp that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that a name with which you are familiar, Witness F?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you that he was, in fact, the man who was the commander of the camp; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that you are incorrect when you allege that Dusko Sikirica was the commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I affirm it and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that he never conducted delegations about the place, delegations of civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: This is what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And he wasn't, was he, present at the closing of the camp, reading out any names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: He was present, he was present, and he read out 120 inmates' names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He certainly wasn't the commander on that day, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know who the commander was, but he read it. He is the one who decided who was going to go. And who the commander above him or underneath him was, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Are you, by your answer, at that point, Witness F, saying that he was not, as far as you know, the commander on the day when those people were sent to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I do not say that, and I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, your evidence is that Dusko Sikirica was the commander of the camp. Are you asserting today that on the day when the camp was closed, that Dusko Sikirica continued to be the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I assert that because he read that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know somebody by the name of Fikret Hedic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If such a person were to suggest or say, rather, that the calling out of the names had been carried out by an army captain first class, you would say that's incorrect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Karanfil Aliskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If he was to assert that it was a man called Kondic who'd called out the names, that would be incorrect, would it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I would say that it was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Returning to Senad Kurbegovic, if he was to assert that the commander of the camp, the entire camp was Zivko Knezevic, who he knew before the war, he'd be wrong about that, would he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That is his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help us about this, please, Witness F: In your handwritten statement, you described on two occasions Dusko Sikirica and you use this phrase "commander of all the guards". What I suggest to you is that the role that Dusko Sikirica played in Keraterm was commander of security, not commander of the shifts, not commander of the guards who were inside the camp, but commander of security. That's the position. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in these military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I can finish even if we go slightly past ten past 4.00 I think that's a sensible thing rather than have a dribble move over into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't want to start gabbling and hurrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, I suggest to you that he was not present on the day after the incident in Room 3 at all. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In evidence you told us today that at the time when these events were taking place, he was around 30ish in age.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: That is -- that was my estimate. Now he looks twice that age, as if he were 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, the name of the person with whom you were friendly at school, who you believed married him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you tell us, please, what the name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, Mira Sekulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And at which school were you and she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: The construction technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On the map which you have produced of the camp, you have put the words "military prison". Is that a place where Serb prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How many prisoners were kept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: I don't know. We had no access there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you hear nothing -- nothing about it whilst you were there, no information given to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Who was to give us the information?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The -- just help us about this, please, Witness F. The total number of people detained at Keraterm whilst you were there, can you tell us, roughly speaking, how many they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: 1.000 to 1.200. Each room contained 300 to 400 or 200. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were people released from the camp whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Where were they releasing them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: From Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Sometimes they would line up and call out names and they would take people away, but they were not releasing anyone so far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would this be correct, Witness F, that during your time at Keraterm, you and the other more than 1.000 prisoners were at all times in the power of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And they could have killed you at any time, you and all your fellow detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I just want to return briefly to the issue of the title and function of Dusko Sikirica. Could you please just have a look at a copy of a document, please. Having looked at it, could you perhaps put it on the monitor. There are some copies for my learned friends and for the Court in the English version thereof. Witness F, firstly can you tell us, please, have you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you just do one thing with me, please, would you look at the bottom right-hand corner and just indicate it by putting your finger on it on the monitor, do you see in the bottom right-hand corner in your language, I think, a signature right at the bottom and some typed words written above it; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to read out what is written there, please, nothing else, just that corner signature and note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: "Record compiled by commander of the Keraterm security."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Signed Dusko Sikirica, is that right, or it appears to be signed Dusko Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: Dusko Sikirica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Does that refresh your memory in any way, Witness F, as to the proper title and role of Dusko Sikirica in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS F
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much for letting me go slightly past ten past 4.00, Your Honour. It's most kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Greaves. We are going to take the adjournment now and we will resume on Monday morning at 9.30. Witness F, you are reminded that during the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 4.13 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday the 2nd day of April, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25
